# SK2213 — The `IndexOf` result is compared to a positive number

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A search that reports absence as `-1` is tested with `> 0`, which also rejects a match at the first position.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S2692 |

## Why

`IndexOf` answers two questions at once: whether the value is there, and where. `> 0` conflates them, and the element at position 0 falls down the gap — present, and reported absent. It survives every test whose fixture does not begin with the needle, which is most of them, and fails the day a caller passes a string that starts with what it is looking for. `>= 0` is the test for presence and `Contains` says it without an index at all. ⚠ **This is the carve-out SK2053 names and declines.** SK2053 proves a comparison from the framework contract that a count is never negative; `IndexOf` is the framework member whose negative result is *meaningful*, which is why SK2053's own false-positive note excludes it and why the two can never report the same expression. SK2001 is further away still: it decides a comparison from the operand type's range, and `IndexOf` returns an `int`, whose range settles nothing about zero.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (path.IndexOf(':') > 0) { Split(path); }
```

Write:

```csharp
if (path.IndexOf(':') >= 0) { Split(path); }
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **`> 0` is a correct test when "found, but not at the start" is what was meant**, and the rule cannot tell the two apart — which is why the fix is offered as one to review rather than one `skala fix` applies unasked. The escape hatch is spelling it unambiguously: `>= 1` says "found at or after position 1" with no second reading, and is deliberately **not** reported, so a codebase that means it can say so once and never see the rule again. `>= 0`, `!= -1`, `== -1` and `< 0` are the correct spellings of presence and absence and none of them is reported. ⚠ **Only a closed set of search methods is covered**, each of which is documented to return `-1` for absence: `IndexOf`, `LastIndexOf`, `IndexOfAny` and `LastIndexOfAny` on `string`; the static `Array.IndexOf` and `Array.LastIndexOf`; `IndexOf` and `LastIndexOf` on `List<T>`, on `IList<T>` and on the `System.Collections.IList` interface; and the `MemoryExtensions` span searches. A method called `IndexOf` on a type outside that set may return anything at all and is not reported — the same reasoning that stops SK2053 trusting a hand-written `Count`. The constant must be the literal `0` on either side, so `0 < s.IndexOf(c)` is reported and `n < s.IndexOf(c)` is not. The fix replaces the `>` operator token with `>=` and touches nothing else. Generated code is excluded.
